content: In pregnancy, the term quickening refers to the first time a pregnant woman perceives or feels the movement of the fetus within her uterus. The Oxford English Dictionary defines to quicken as reaching the stage of pregnancy where the fetus shows signs of life. In the 20th century, the advent of ultrasound technology allowed for the visualization of fetal movement even before the pregnant woman could feel it, adding complexity to the concept of quickening. The initial sensation of quickening is often described as a light tapping or a fluttering sensation, similar to the movement of a butterfly. As the pregnancy progresses, these sensations become stronger and more regular. Early fetal movements are sometimes mistaken for gas or hunger pangs. The uterine muscles, rather than the abdominal muscles, are the first to detect fetal motion. Consequently, a woman’s body weight generally does not significantly influence when these movements are first perceived. Women who have previously given birth tend to have more relaxed uterine muscles, making them more sensitive to fetal motion. For these women, fetal movements can sometimes be felt as early as 14 weeks into the pregnancy. Typically, quickening occurs naturally around the midpoint of pregnancy, with multiparous women (those who have had previous pregnancies) often feeling movements around 18 weeks. Historically, quickening has been regarded as a significant milestone, sometimes considered the point at which the fetus attains individual life. In the 18th century, British legal scholar William Blackstone discussed quickening in the context of feticide and abortion. However, quickening was only one of several historical standards used to determine when the right to life attaches to a fetus. According to ancient law, as described by Blackstone, another standard was the formation of the fetus, which occurs weeks before quickening. Henry Bracton, writing about 500 years before Blackstone, also referenced this ancient law. The idea that a fetus was considered alive upon formation dates back at least another millennium. In the Septuagint version of the Old Testament, the formation of the fetus was emphasized over quickening, as seen in the Book of Exodus. In the early Judeo-Christian tradition, the highest value for life was thought to accrue when the fetus was formed. Over time, the moment of quickening became the predominant standard for determining the right to life. Eventually, the concept of fetal viability—when the fetus can survive outside the womb—gained greater significance. In some contexts, the moment of conception has also been used as a standard for when the right to life legally attaches to a human being.
